There are lots of different roles. If you are a poll watcher, you are essentially a volunteer for your political party. You will sit at the polling place with a list of all the voters in that precinct and mark off when people vote. After a few hours, another volunteer will pick up the list and start calling people who haven't voted yet. At the end of the day, you will observe as the election workers at that precinct count the ballots and seal them up. If you want, you can go to the central hub where the ballots are taken afterward (it is the county courthouse where I live) and watch them count them all in real time. You can also attend the official canvass, when the provisional ballots are counted. It's normally a week or so after the election.

There are several things you can't do, though. You can't wear anything that references a specific candidate and you can't try to intimidate voters or convince them to vote a certain way when you're actually at the polling place. Most poll watchers just wear red or blue.

The specific rules vary by state. Where I live, you have to be appointed as a poll agent by a candidate or party and you have to wear a badge that says "Observer," which the election officials will give you. If you contact your local party (I'm assuming Republican), they will be happy to set you up and train you on what you need to know. They will almost certainly have lawyers for you to call if you see anything fishy that needs to be documented for a potential lawsuit.

This is a perfectly ordinary part of the political process and a critical role that local parties play. If you want to do it independently of a party, you'll have a harder time, but it's not impossible.

I'm an election judge for the first time this election - were went over what the observers do briefly.

During the open poll hours, you are there to observe if there is any funny business, but what I think is most important, is if anyone needs help actually voting, one observer from each party(to make sure neither is coaching the voter who to vote for) comes over to help them actually fill in the dots on the ballot, or help them read it. Think elderly or different disability levels.

You also watch us set up the poll machine to make sure there is no fuckery, and count at the end too.

Every poll precinct needs 2 of these, so you will most likely be needed.
